name: Oral cyproterone acetate
lead: Cyproterone acetate (CPA) is a steroidal antiandrogen and progestin sold alone as Androcur and, combined with ethinylestradiol, as Diane-35, Dianette and similar products.[1] For hair, it is used in some countries as an off-label or labelled treatment for scalp hair loss, hirsutism, acne and seborrhea in women with androgen-related signs.[1][2]

It was first synthesised at Schering in 1961 and reached the market as an antiandrogen in Europe in 1973; it has never been marketed in the United States.[1] Documented risks include liver toxicity, blood clots and meningioma, and the European Medicines Agency issued a warning in 2020 about meningioma at higher doses.[1] Because of its effects on male hormones, use for hair loss in men is described as generally impractical.[1]
infobox: Prescription only; not marketed in the US

paras: Wikipedia lists acne, hirsutism, seborrhea, scalp hair loss and hidradenitis suppurativa in women among its uses, usually as a low-dose combined pill with ethinylestradiol.[1] It reports that a low-dose pill improved acne in 75 to 90 percent of women and that up to 70 percent relapsed after stopping.[1]

A registered European survey (NCT04925180) of physician awareness of Androcur and cyproterone safety information names androgenisation signs in women, including hirsutism, androgenetic alopecia, acne and seborrhea, among the treatment contexts.[3]

The drug is also used for polycystic ovary syndrome and other androgen excess states, in feminizing hormone therapy (WPATH SOC8 recommends no more than 10 mg a day), and at high doses for prostate cancer and to reduce sex drive in paraphilias.[1]

CPA blocks the androgen receptor, is a progestogen that suppresses gonadotropins, and has weak glucocorticoid activity but no estrogenic activity; oral bioavailability is 68 to 100 percent and it is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4.[1] Its progestin pharmacology is reviewed in a 2003 Maturitas classification of progestins.[4]
Grokipedia's page concerns the related parent compound cyproterone, not the acetate; it describes CPA as the ester that gained progestogenic and antigonadotropic activity.[5]

Wikipedia lists gynecomastia, reduced libido and erectile dysfunction in men, fatigue, depression and weight gain at high doses, and rarer liver toxicity (including failure and tumors), raised prolactin, blood clots and meningioma.[1] Abrupt discontinuation of high doses can cause adrenal insufficiency, and pregnancy, liver disease, prior thromboembolism and meningioma are contraindications.[1]

The EMA warned in 2020 that doses of 25 mg a day or more may increase meningioma risk and recommended alternatives where possible, except for prostate cancer.[1] Two 2009 BMJ studies of hormonal contraception and venous thromboembolism compared risk by progestogen type and oestrogen dose, and reported higher risk with pills containing cyproterone acetate than with some other progestogens.[6][7]

Registered studies include trials of cyproterone-containing pills in polycystic ovary syndrome, hyperandrogenism and menstrual disorders, and a bioequivalence study.[8][9][10] No placebo-controlled trial of oral cyproterone acetate for androgenetic alopecia is cited here; effectiveness for scalp hair is described mainly in reviews and clinical practice.

CPA was synthesised in 1961 by Rudolf Wiechert at Schering, was first approved as an antiandrogen in Europe in 1973 and as the contraceptive Diane in 1978; Canada followed in 1987.[1] Wikipedia reports that it was never marketed in the US, reportedly because of concerns about breast tumors in beagles and teratogenicity.[1] It is prescription only, widely available elsewhere, and used internationally under many brand names.[1]

card.summary: Prescription antiandrogen used abroad for women's hair loss, acne and hirsutism, with liver, clot and meningioma risks.
card.note: Not marketed in the US; EMA warned in 2020 about meningioma at doses of 25 mg/day or more.

quick.overview:
Oral cyproterone acetate is a hormonal drug that blocks androgen receptors and acts as a progestin. In Europe and elsewhere it is prescribed to women for acne, excess hair growth and androgen-related scalp hair loss, often in a pill with ethinylestradiol.

It is not sold in the US and is generally considered impractical for men because of its hormonal effects.
quick.mechanism: It blocks androgen receptors, suppresses pituitary gonadotropins through its progestogenic action and so lowers androgen production, and is broken down mainly by the liver enzyme CYP3A4.
quick.risks: Documented risks include liver toxicity, venous blood clots, meningioma (EMA warning, 2020) and adrenal insufficiency on abrupt stop of high doses. Pregnancy, liver disease and prior clots are contraindications. It is prescription only.
